figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of explanations. Left: raw – Concept fragmented, noisy explanation. Middle: words – Subwords merged into words. Right: smart_depth – “saddle embolus” as one concept, a clean explanation.

Figure 5: Visual explanation comparison for the long caption containing “the right kidney”. Left: words strategy – Fragmentation leads to the inability to distinguish between the kidneys. Right: noun_chunks – Semantic grouping unifies these tokens, assigning importance directly to the right kidney.

Figure 6: Visual explanation comparison for the caption “Head CT demonstrating left parotiditis”. Left: raw – Fragmenting the concept into “left”, “parotid”, and “itis” results in scattered attention. Right: smart_depth – Processing “left parotiditis” as a single semantic unit yields a precise explanation. Semantic grouping eliminates the noise seen with fragmented tokens.

Figure 7: Visual explanation comparison for “massive cardiomegaly”. Left: raw – Fragmentation of the medical term generates significant visual noise outside the heart region. Right: smart_depth — Processing the entire phrase as a single unit eliminates noise.
Figure 12: True label. Left: raw. Right: smart_depth.
Figure 13: False label. Left: raw. Right: smart_depth.

Figure 8: Visual explanation comparison for “Sagittal view of the calcified nasal packing”. Left: raw – Noisy distribution of importance. Right: smart_depth – Clear semantic grounding where relevant image parts receive positive attribution.
Figure 9: Visual grounding of explicit annotations. The word “arrow” is connected to the red graphical marker pointing towards the spinal pathology.
Figure 1: Faithfulness evaluation on 128 short captions samples. Left: Spearman Rank Correlation. Right: Adjusted 𝑅2. noun_chunks and smart_depth consistently outperform the token-level baselines.
Figure 11: Image transformation comparison. Left: Upside down raw. Right: Upside down smart_depth.
Figure 10: Image transformation comparison. Left: Normal raw. Right: Normal smart_depth.

Figure 2: Goodness-of-fit metrics on long captions. Left: Standard 𝑅2 shows comparable explanatory potential. Right: Adjusted 𝑅2 reveals the inefficiency of the raw strategy, which is penalized for its high feature count, whereas smart_depth remains robust due to semantic parsimony.

Figure 3: Insertion and Deletion curves. Left: Short Captions (< 10 words). Semantic grouping outperforms raw tokens on short texts. Right: Long Captions (> 30 words). On long texts, the raw baseline tracks scattered attention to background noise, slightly inflating its AID score compared to semantic grouping.
